modules.title: Java values, expressions and string methods
modules.focus: Trace type conversion before recording an output.
explanation: Java evaluates expressions according to operand types and precedence. Dividing two int values performs integer division. Assigning that result to a double afterwards does not restore the discarded fraction; a floating-point operand is needed before division.

String objects provide methods such as length and substring. Indices start at zero, and substring(start,end) includes start but excludes end. Method contracts specify which inputs are valid and what result or state change a call produces.

workedExample.prompt: Compare double a=7/2; with double b=7/2.0;.
steps: In the first expression both operands are int, so division produces 3 before conversion: a=3.0.
The second expression uses a double operand, so b=3.5.

misconception.claim: The destination variable alone decides how division is performed.
misconception.correction: Operand types determine the division before assignment.

questions.hint: Find the remainder after whole groups of 5.

questions.prompt: Evaluate double x=11/4; and double y=11/4.0;.
For String s="vertex", evaluate s.substring(2,5) and state s afterwards.

notes.title: Reasoning through java values, expressions and string methods
paragraphs: Java evaluates an expression using the operand types present at that moment. Assigning an integer-division result to a double does not recover the discarded fraction. Cast an operand before division when a fractional result is required. String indexes start at zero and substring uses an inclusive start with an exclusive end. Strings are immutable: a method such as substring returns a value without modifying the original string. Trace the type and value of each intermediate expression, especially when arithmetic and string concatenation appear together in a single statement.

workedExamples.prompt: Evaluate String s="score:"+2+3 and double x=(double)9/4.
steps: String concatenation proceeds left to right, giving "score:2" then "score:23".
Casting 9 before division makes the numeric calculation floating point.

flashcards.front: When must a cast occur to avoid integer division?
What is the last included index in substring(a,b)?
Does a String method mutate the original string?

modules.title: Trace loops with boundary cases
modules.focus: Record state after each executed iteration.
explanation: A loop has an initial state, a continuation condition, a body and an update. Check the condition before each iteration of a while or for loop. Inclusive and exclusive bounds change how often the body executes.

Boolean expressions control selection. Short-circuit evaluation of && can guard an unsafe operation on its right. To test an algorithm, include empty, smallest valid, boundary and ordinary cases, since a single successful trace cannot establish general correctness.

steps: The body runs for i=1,2,3,4, producing totals 1,3,6,10.
When i becomes 5, i<5 is false. The final total is 10.

misconception.claim: A loop with i<5 includes i=5.
misconception.correction: The strict inequality stops before that iteration.

questions.prompt: What final count results from int c=0; for(int i=0;i<=6;i+=2){c++;}?
questions.hint: List the values of i that enter the body.
checkpoints: Count iterations, not the final i.

questions.prompt: Rewrite !(x<3 || x>8) as an equivalent range test.

checkpoints: The next value 11 fails the bound.
hints: The next value 11 fails the bound.

questions.hint: At i=a.length the bound test is false.
questions.prompt: Why is i<a.length && a[i]>0 safer than a[i]>0 && i<a.length when i may equal a.length, assuming i≥0?
questions.answer: The first condition checks the upper bound before accessing a[i].
checkpoints: At i=a.length the bound test is false.
Reversing the order accesses an invalid index first.
hints: At i=a.length the bound test is false.

notes.title: Reasoning through trace loops with boundary cases
paragraphs: A loop trace should record the initial state, condition check, body and update in that order. A strict bound and an inclusive bound can differ by one complete iteration. A loop invariant is a property maintained at each relevant checkpoint, such as a running total equalling the sum of values already visited. Termination needs progress toward a false condition; changing the wrong variable can create an infinite loop. Boolean short-circuiting can protect a later expression from invalid access, provided the safety check appears first in the condition.

workedExamples.prompt: Trace int n=13; int steps=0; while(n>1){n/=2;steps++;}.
steps: Integer division changes n from 13 to 6, then 3, then 1.
Each body execution increments steps.
At n=1 the condition is false.
workedExamples.conclusion: The final state is n=1 and steps=3.

flashcards.front: When is a while condition checked?

flashcards.back: A property preserved at specified points across iterations.
An update that never makes the condition false.

flashcards.front: Why put an index check before array access in &&?
flashcards.back: Short-circuiting skips unsafe access when the check is false.

modules.title: Classes that protect their own state
modules.focus: Separate object state from method parameters.
explanation: A class combines attributes with operations that manage them. Private instance variables restrict direct access from other classes. A constructor establishes the starting state, while methods expose intentional behaviour and can protect invariants.

Each object has its own instance state. A static field instead belongs to the class. When a parameter shadows an instance variable, this.field names the object’s field explicitly; assigning the parameter to itself leaves the field unchanged.

workedExample.prompt: Why does a constructor Counter(int count){this.count=count;} initialise an instance field correctly?
steps: The parameter count is the supplied value; this.count identifies the field of the newly constructed object.
The assignment transfers the parameter value to that field, rather than assigning the parameter to itself.

misconception.claim: Two objects of the same class must share every instance field.
misconception.correction: They share a class definition but ordinarily have separate instance state.

questions.prompt: Two Counter objects start at 0. Calling increment on only the first adds 1 to its instance count. Give both counts.
questions.hint: Track the receiver of the method call.
checkpoints: Only the first object is mutated.
The field is an instance field.

questions.prompt: Why might a setBalance method reject a negative argument while the balance field stays private?
questions.answer: It can preserve a nonnegative-balance rule by controlling every permitted update.
checkpoints: Explain how private access prevents bypassing it from another class.

questions.hint: The first request exceeds 8 and is rejected.
questions.prompt: A private balance is 8. withdraw(n) changes it only when n≥0 and n≤balance. What follows withdraw(10), then withdraw(3)?
checkpoints: The first request exceeds 8 and is rejected.
hints: The first request exceeds 8 and is rejected.

questions.hint: Only the receiver’s instance count changes.
questions.prompt: Two distinct objects have instance count=0 and share static total=0. Each increment adds one to its count and to total. Increment the first twice. Give both counts and total.
questions.answer: First count 2, second count 0, shared total 2.
checkpoints: Only the receiver’s instance count changes.
The second object has not received an increment.
Each of the two calls increments the shared total.
hints: Only the receiver’s instance count changes.
The second object has not received an increment.

notes.title: Reasoning through classes that protect their own state
paragraphs: An object’s instance fields represent its own state, while static fields are shared by all instances of a class. Encapsulation controls permitted state changes through constructors and methods. A private field is not sufficient by itself: every mutating method must preserve the intended invariant. Constructor parameters can shadow fields, making this.field useful to distinguish the receiver’s state. Passing an object reference copies the reference, not the object; two variables may therefore refer to the same mutable instance. A method can mutate that instance without changing which object the caller’s variable references.

workedExamples.prompt: A Box has a private int count=2 and add(int n){count+=n;}. Variables a and b reference the same Box. After a.add(3), what does b read?
steps: Both variables identify one instance rather than two copies.
The method changes that instance’s count from 2 to 5.
Access through b reads the updated field.
workedExamples.conclusion: b reads 5 because a and b are aliases.

flashcards.front: What state is shared by all instances?

flashcards.back: Two references identify the same object.
Each state-changing path must preserve the invariant.

modules.title: Collections and safe traversal
modules.focus: Visit each valid element without skipping shifted entries.
explanation: An array’s valid indices run from zero to length-1. Traversals often maintain an accumulator, such as a sum or best value. A two-dimensional array is an array of rows, so a robust traversal uses each row’s own length.

Removing an ArrayList element shifts later elements left. A forward loop that increments immediately after removal can skip the next item; walking backwards avoids that shift problem. Binary search additionally requires sorted data, unlike a linear scan.

workedExample.prompt: Compute the sum of int[] a={3,1,4} using a loop.
steps: Initialise sum=0 and traverse i from 0 while i<a.length.
Add 3, then 1, then 4. The final sum is 8, and index 3 is never accessed.

misconception.claim: Binary search works on any unsorted list.
misconception.correction: It relies on sorted order to eliminate half the remaining search range.

questions.prompt: What is the last valid index of an array with length 7?
A list is [2,4,5]. Removing each even value with a forward loop skips 4 after removing 2. Explain a repair.
questions.answer: Traverse from the last index backwards, or do not advance after a removal.
checkpoints: Ensure the shifted element is examined.

questions.hint: Each x is a copy of a primitive element value.
questions.prompt: Trace int[] a={2,5}; for(int x:a){x*=2;}. What is a afterwards?
checkpoints: Each x is a copy of a primitive element value.
Multiplying x changes only the loop variable.
No assignment is made to a[i].
hints: Each x is a copy of a primitive element value.
Multiplying x changes only the loop variable.

questions.prompt: An ArrayList is [1,2,2,3]. Remove every 2 by traversing backward. State the removal indexes and result.
questions.answer: Remove indexes 2 then 1; the result is [1,3].
checkpoints: Index 1 still contains the other 2 and is removed.

notes.title: Reasoning through collections and safe traversal
paragraphs: An array’s length is fixed after creation, whereas an ArrayList can change size. Both use zero-based indexes, but their access syntax differs. Removing an ArrayList element shifts later elements left, so an increasing-index loop can skip a newly shifted element. Backward traversal avoids that particular skip because unvisited lower indexes do not move. A search should specify what happens for an empty collection or missing target. Enhanced for loops are useful for reading values, but assigning the loop variable does not replace primitive values stored in the original array.

workedExamples.prompt: Find the maximum of a nonempty array [−7,−2,−9] without assuming values are positive.
steps: Initialise max to the first element, −7.
Compare −2 and update max to −2.
Compare −9 and leave max unchanged.
workedExamples.conclusion: The maximum is −2; initialising to zero would be incorrect.

flashcards.front: Why is zero a poor universal initial maximum?
flashcards.back: All stored numbers may be negative.
Later elements shift one index left.

flashcards.front: What is the first valid index?
Does assigning an int enhanced-for variable update the array?
